title: The Letter of Aristeas
ask_addressed: Quote the primary evidence for how the Hebrew Bible reached Greek and Latin readers
quote: Demetrius of Phalerum, the president of the king's library, received vast sums of money
summary: The Letter's own framing: the Torah is translated because Ptolemy's librarian wants it for the royal library; Demetrius says Hebrew letters and dialect need translation.
limits: Narrative is presented by a fictional Greek courtier; the Jewish Encyclopedia (separate candidate) shows Demetrius could not have been in office under Philadelphus. Story, not evidence for the actual process.

text.edition: Charles, ed., The Apocrypha and Pseudepigrapha of the Old Testament, vol. 2 (Clarendon Press, 1913), English translation, as hosted at CCEL (edition year per Bible Blender page seen in search snippet only).

composition.basis: Jewish Encyclopedia (Schürer: c. 200 BCE; the encyclopedia itself argues for the later Maccabean period); date is disputed, treated here as 2nd c. BCE. Opened: https://www.jewishencyclopedia.com/articles/1765-aristeas-letter-of

text.witness: Greek manuscripts are medieval (a Vatican copy of 11th c. CE is pictured on the Wikipedia Septuagint page, opened); no ancient copy of the Letter was opened. Quoted via R.H. Charles translation (Oxford: Clarendon, 1913) as hosted by CCEL.

title: Wisdom of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus), Prologue
ask_addressed: Quote the primary evidence for how the Hebrew Bible reached Greek and Latin readers
quote: in the eight and thirtieth year coming into Egypt, when Euergetes was king, and continuing there some time
summary: The grandson dates his arrival in Egypt to the 38th year of a King Euergetes and says he translated his grandfather's book there.
limits: Which Euergetes is meant is a dating question not resolved from sources opened; a KJV-era English rendering is quoted, not the Greek.

text.work: Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus), Prologue by the translator
text.edition: King James Bible Apocrypha (1611), as transcribed on English Wikisource

composition.basis: Jewish Encyclopedia (opened) says Sirach was 'probably' translated in the year 130 BCE; task brief and conventional reading of the 38th year of Euergetes give 132 BCE. The identification of Euergetes (III or VIII) was not checked in a source I opened.

text.witness: Earliest witness for the Greek not established from sources opened. Hebrew Sirach survives at Qumran (2Q18, 11QPs-a), Masada and the Cairo Geniza per Wikipedia Septuagint page (opened).

title: Jerome on the Canon of Scripture (Prologus Galeatus)
authors: Jerome; trans. Fremantle, W.H., modified by M.D.M.
ask_addressed: Quote the primary evidence for how the Hebrew Bible reached Greek and Latin readers
quote: the book of Jesus the Son of Sirach, and Judith, and Tobias, and the Shepherd [of Hermes?] are not in the canon
summary: Jerome excludes the books outside the Hebrew canon from the canon; Sirach, the book whose prologue is quoted above, is one of them.
limits: A statement about Jerome's own preference; later church practice differed (not examined here).
